title: Unitree files for Shanghai IPO seeking $904M to scale G1, H1 and R1 humanoids
subtitle: The Hangzhou robotics company that already sells adult-sized humanoids for the price of a used car aims to raise 6.1 billion yuan to move from viral demos to volume manufacturing.
author: AESOP AI Engine
body: Chinese humanoid-robotics maker Unitree is preparing a Shanghai STAR Market listing seeking roughly 6.1 billion yuan (~$904 million), one of the largest robotics IPOs on a mainland exchange to date. The Hangzhou-based company already ships the G1 humanoid at prices well below Western competitors, the larger H1, and the industrial R1 platform. Proceeds are earmarked for volume manufacturing, R&D on whole-body control policies, and expansion of its component supply chain — the actuators, harmonic drives and force-torque sensors that are the real bottleneck in humanoid production.

The engineering thesis behind Unitree is unglamorous but decisive: drive down the bill-of-materials cost of a bipedal platform until it slots into the same procurement bracket as an industrial robot arm. That is what makes the videos of G1 dancing or backflipping matter — not the parkour, but the fact the hardware is manufacturable at scale. Software is catching up in parallel, with Google DeepMind's Gemini Robotics 2 whole-body model (July 31) and Meta's Assured Robot Intelligence stack (May 3) pushing the same trend from the policy side.

This lists into a specific competitive moment. Boston Dynamics' Atlas is a research showcase, Figure and Agility Robotics are commercial but expensive, BYD's Xiao Di humanoid was teased for August dealership deployment, and Booster's T2 flagship was released in July. Unitree's edge is that it started at the low end of the market and is climbing up, which historically wins in hardware. A public listing gives it the capital to hold that position and gives Western investors a proxy on Chinese physical-AI progress at a moment when the country is systematically pulling ahead in the robotics-plus-manufacturing stack.

For learners: physical AI is where a lot of the next decade's applied ML work will live, and the interesting problems are at the seam between simulation and reality. Reinforcement learning that works in sim but fails on hardware, sensor noise that policies never saw in training, actuators that behave differently after 10,000 hours — these are the failure modes that separate a viral demo from a shipped product. If you want a career that ages well, working through even one small physical-AI project (a quadruped, a manipulator, a drone) teaches lessons no purely-digital ML project can.
